# Making mods for OpenRAC

OpenRAC plays Ratchet & Clank natively on a PC. A **mod** changes how the game
behaves: a new way to strafe, swapped buttons, a tweak to an enemy. Players
install mods from the OpenRAC launcher's **Mods** tab, by pasting the address
of your repository, and switch them on and off there.

There are two kinds of behaviour mod:

| | Script mod | Native mod |
|---|---|---|
| Written in | [Luau](https://luau.org) (a typed Lua) | C or C++ |
| You need | a text editor | a C/C++ compiler and CMake |
| Runs on | every platform, Android included | the platforms you build it for (the template's workflow builds Windows, Linux and macOS) |
| Safety | sandboxed: it sees only what OpenRAC gives it | runs as code on the player's computer |
| Since | interface 1.1 (SDK 1.1) | interface 1.0 |

Start with a script mod unless you need the speed or the reach of native code.
Mods of textures, models and levels are made with the level editor instead
([editor/MODDING.md](https://github.com/OpenRAC/OpenRAC/blob/master/editor/MODDING.md)).

## Guides

1. [Getting started](getting-started.md): from the template to a mod players can install.
2. [The manifest](manifest.md): `openrac-mod.json`, field by field.
3. [Settings](settings.md): options players change in the launcher.
4. [Hooks](hooks.md): how a mod changes what the game does, and the hook ids that never change.
5. Writing the code:
   - [Script mods (Luau)](scripts.md)
   - [Native mods in C](native-c.md)
   - [Native mods in C++](native-cpp.md)
6. [Packaging and releases](packaging-and-releases.md): the archive, the workflow, tags.
7. [Install from a link](install-from-link.md): what the launcher does with your repository.
8. [Where mods live](where-mods-live.md): the folders and files on a player's computer.
9. [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md): a mod that does not load, purist mode, crash reports.
10. [Views of the game](views.md): extra views for a VR headset or another display, with OpenGL or Vulkan (native mods, interface 1.4).

## Reference

Generated from the SDK's headers, tables and type files by OpenRAC's
[sdk/tools/gen_reference.py](https://github.com/OpenRAC/OpenRAC/blob/master/sdk/tools/gen_reference.py);
never edited by hand:

- [C interface](reference/c-api.md) (`include/openrac/openrac_mod.h`)
- [C++ layer](reference/cpp-api.md) (`include/openrac/mod.hpp`)
- [Luau API](reference/luau-api.md) (`types/rac1.d.luau`)
- [Ratchet & Clank's hook points and fields](reference/hooks-rac1.md)

## What is stable

Stable, and kept working by every OpenRAC of the same interface major version:
the C interface, the manifest, packaging, install from a link, the repository
templates, hook **ids**, and the `openrac` script API.

**Experimental**: anything that names the game's internals: the behaviour
catalogue (moby classes, their update functions and pvars), the fields exposed
to scripts, and the game functions and addresses a native mod looks up itself.
They follow the decompilation and may change. A hook **id** stays, even when
the function behind it is renamed ([hooks](hooks.md#stable-ids)).

How OpenRAC is built inside will get guides of its own after the port's move to
C++. The design notes are in
[docs/port/MODS.md](https://github.com/OpenRAC/OpenRAC/blob/master/docs/port/MODS.md)
(`docs/MODS.md` in the SDK archive, beside these pages).

guides.title: Getting started
guides.markdown:
# Getting started

From nothing to a mod a player installs by pasting a link. Pick a track.

## Script mod (no compiler)

1. **Get the SDK.** Download `openrac-mod-sdk-<version>.zip` from
   [OpenRAC's releases](https://github.com/OpenRAC/OpenRAC/releases) (the ones
   named "Mod SDK") and unpack it. Script mods need SDK 1.1 or later.
2. **Copy the template.** `template-script/` is a whole repository: copy it
   to a new folder and make it a git repository (`git init`).
3. **Name your mod.** In `openrac-mod.json`, set `id` (lower case and
   hyphens, such as `big-jump`), `name`, `author`, `description` and
   `version` ([the manifest](manifest.md)).
4. **Write it.** `main.luau` runs once when the game starts; it takes its
   hooks and callbacks there:

   ```lua
   openrac.on_frame(function()
       if openrac.fields.bolts > 1000 then
           openrac.log("rich!")
       end
   end)
   ```

   [Script mods](scripts.md) has the rest. Point your editor's Luau language
   server at the SDK's `types/rac1.d.luau` for autocomplete (the template's
   `.vscode/settings.json` does it for VS Code with luau-lsp).
5. **Try it.** In the launcher's **Mods** tab, **Add a mod**, and choose your
   folder. Switch it on and press Play. Your `openrac.log` lines are in the
   game's log (**Logs** on the game's page).
6. **Release it.** Push the repository to GitHub (public), then a tag with
   the manifest's version:

   ```sh
   git tag v0.1.0
   git push origin v0.1.0
   ```

   The template's workflow packages the mod and publishes the release
   ([packaging and releases](packaging-and-releases.md)).
7. **Share the link.** Players paste `https://github.com/<you>/<repo>` in the
   Mods tab's **Add from a link** ([install from a link](install-from-link.md)).

## Native mod (C or C++)

1. **Get the SDK** as above, and the tools: CMake, Ninja, and a compiler
   (Xcode's command-line tools on macOS, `build-essential` on Linux, Visual
   Studio with "Desktop development with C++" on Windows).
2. **Copy the template.** `template/` is a whole repository for a C++ mod.
3. **Fetch the SDK it pins, and build:**

   ```sh
   python3 tools/fetch_sdk.py      # the SDK sdk.lock names, into .sdk/ (commit sdk.lock after the first time)
   cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
   cmake --build build
   ```

4. **Write it** in `src/mod.cpp` ([in C++](native-cpp.md), or [in C](native-c.md)):

   ```cpp
   #include "openrac/mod.hpp"
   #include "openrac/games/rac1.hpp"

   static void load(openrac::Mod& mod) {
       mod.hook<openrac::rac1::Hero_SetPlanarVelocity>([](auto original, float angle) {
           original(angle);   // the game's own, or the mod loaded before yours
       });
   }
   OPENRAC_MOD_CPP("my-mod", "0.1.0", load)
   ```

5. **Try it.** **Add a mod** in the launcher with the folder
   `build/package/<target>`, switch it on, Play.
6. **Release it** with a tag, as for a script mod: the workflow builds it on
   Windows, Linux and macOS and publishes one archive per platform with their
   checksums. Players never need a compiler.

## Next

- [Hooks](hooks.md): what you can change, and how mods share a hook.
- [Settings](settings.md): give players options.
- [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md): when the mod does not load.

guides.title: The manifest: `openrac-mod.json
guides.markdown:
# The manifest: `openrac-mod.json`

Every mod has one, at the top of its folder. The launcher reads it to show the
mod and decide whether it can run; the game reads it again at start. Both apply
the same rules, and the SDK's `tools/package_mod.py --check openrac-mod.json`
checks a manifest the same way.

## A script mod

```json
{
  "format": 2,
  "id": "button-swap",
  "name": "Button swap",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": "Your name",
  "description": "Swaps two buttons of the pad.",
  "license": "MIT",
  "homepage": "https://github.com/you/your-mods",
  "type": "script",
  "api": "1.1",
  "scripts": ["main.luau"],
  "games": { "rac1": ["pal", "ntsc"] },
  "settings": [
    { "key": "pair", "name": "Buttons", "type": "choice", "default": "cross-square",
      "choices": [ { "value": "cross-square", "name": "Cross and Square" },
                   { "value": "l1-r1", "name": "L1 and R1" } ] }
  ]
}
```

## A native mod

```json
{
  "format": 2,
  "id": "lock-strafe",
  "name": "Lock-strafe",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": "OpenRAC contributors",
  "description": "Strafe as in the later games.",
  "api": "1.0",
  "games": { "rac1": ["pal", "ntsc"] },
  "plugin": {
    "macos-arm64": "lib/macos-arm64/lock_strafe.dylib",
    "linux-x86_64": "lib/linux-x86_64/lock_strafe.so",
    "windows-x86_64": "lib/windows-x86_64/lock_strafe.dll"
  },
  "hooks": ["rac1.pad.process_report", "rac1.player.turn_to_heading"]
}
```

You do not write `plugin` by hand: the SDK's CMake (`openrac_add_mod`) fills in
the platform it built, and `package_mod.py --merge` joins the platforms
([packaging](packaging-and-releases.md)).

## Fields

| Field | Required | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `format` | yes | `2`. (A file with `"format": 1` is a data pack of textures, models or levels, made by the level editor.) |
| `id` | yes | Lower-case letters, digits and single hyphens, at most 64 characters: `big-jump`. It never changes between versions: the launcher replaces an installed mod of the same id. |
| `name` | yes | What players see. |
| `version` | yes | `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, optionally `-suffix` (`1.2.0`, `2.0.0-beta`). Raise it for each release: updates compare versions. |
| `author`, `description`, `license` | no | Shown in the launcher. |
| `homepage` | no | An `https://` address, shown as the mod's source. |
| `type` | no | `"native"` (the default) or `"script"`. |
| `api` | yes | The mod interface you wrote for, `MAJOR.MINOR`: `"1.0"` for native mods, `"1.1"` or later for script mods. A game whose interface has another major version, or a lower minor, does not load the mod and says why. |
| `games` | yes | The game and the discs the mod is for: `{"rac1": ["pal", "ntsc"]}` (PAL and NTSC-U). |
| `scripts` | script mods | The `.luau` files to run at start, in order, as paths inside the mod (forward slashes). |
| `plugin` | native mods | Platform to library path inside the mod. Platforms: `macos-arm64`, `macos-x86_64`, `linux-x86_64`, `linux-aarch64`, `windows-x86_64`, `windows-arm64`, `android-arm64`. |
| `hooks` | no | The hook points the mod takes, by id (`rac1.player.take_damage`) or alias (`Hero_TakeDamage`) ([hooks](hooks.md)). `package_mod.py` checks each against the SDK's table of the mod's games. The launcher shows which mods share a hook point. |
| `settings` | no | Options for players ([settings](settings.md)). |
| `vulkan_device` | no | `true` for a native mod of `api` 1.4 or later that makes the Vulkan device with the port (`setup_vulkan`, [views](views.md)): the mods then load before the window opens. Ignored otherwise. |
| `requires` | no | Mods that must be on, and load before this one: `[{"id": "other-mod", "version": ">=1.2.0"}]` (`version` is `>=X.Y.Z`, `=X.Y.Z`, or left out). |
| `conflicts` | no | Mods it cannot run with: `[{"id": "other-strafe", "reason": "both take L2 and R2"}]`. |
| `load` | no | Order hints: `{"after": ["camera-tweaks"], "before": []}`. The launcher places the mod accordingly when it is switched on. |

## What gets a mod refused

The launcher shows the reason on the mod's row, and the game writes it to
`status.json` ([troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md)):

- another game or disc than the one played;
- an `api` the game's interface does not cover;
- a native mod with no library for this computer's platform;
- a mod it `requires` that is missing, off, too old, or later in the list;
- a conflict with a mod that is on (either mod may list the other).

guides.title: Settings
guides.markdown:
# Settings

Settings are options a player changes in the launcher's Mods tab, under your
mod's row. You declare them in the manifest; the launcher draws the controls,
keeps the values, and the game hands them to your mod at start. A change counts
from the game's next start.

## Declaring them

```json
"settings": [
  { "key": "mode", "name": "Mode", "type": "choice", "default": "lock",
    "choices": [ { "value": "lock", "name": "Lock with weapons" },
                 { "value": "hold", "name": "Hold L2 or R2" } ],
    "description": "How the strafe starts." },
  { "key": "trace", "name": "Trace", "type": "bool", "default": false },
  { "key": "every", "name": "Log every", "type": "int", "default": 10, "min": 1, "max": 600 },
  { "key": "scale", "name": "Speed", "type": "float", "default": 1.0, "min": 0.5, "max": 3.0, "step": 0.1 },
  { "key": "greeting", "name": "Greeting", "type": "string", "default": "hi", "max_length": 40 }
]
```

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `key` | lower case, digits and `_`: what your code asks for |
| `name` | the label players see |
| `type` | `bool`, `int`, `float`, `choice`, `string` or `keybind` (interface 1.2) |
| `default` | the value until the player changes it |
| `description` | one line under the label (optional) |
| `min`, `max` | `int` and `float` |
| `step` | `float` |
| `choices` | `choice`: two or more `{"value", "name"}` |
| `max_length` | `string` |
| `binds` | `keybind`: how many inputs it takes, 1 or 2 (2 when absent) |
| `group` | `keybind`: keybinds of the same group may not share an input (the launcher warns); of different groups they may |

The launcher shows a switch for `bool`, a segmented control or a list for
`choice`, "press a key" buttons for `keybind`, and a field for the others.

## Key bindings

A `keybind` (interface 1.2: `"api": "1.2"`) holds up to two inputs as
names, comma-separated: `"KeyF,MouseMiddle"`, or `""` for none. Keys are
named by where they are on the keyboard, as the web's `KeyboardEvent.code`
names them (`KeyW`, `Digit1`, `Space`, `ShiftLeft`, `ArrowUp`, `Numpad0`,
`F5`); the mouse's are `MouseLeft`, `MouseRight`, `MouseMiddle`, `MouseBack`
and `MouseForward`, the wheel's `WheelUp`, `WheelDown`, `WheelLeft` and
`WheelRight`. `openrac/keys.h` has the whole table and turns a name into
what `input()` reports (see [native mods in C](native-c.md)).

```json
{ "key": "jump", "name": "Jump", "type": "keybind", "default": "Space", "group": "play" },
{ "key": "menu_back", "name": "Menu: back", "type": "keybind", "default": "Backspace", "group": "menu" }
```

## Presets

Presets (interface 1.2) set several settings at once, of any type: sliders,
choices, switches, text and keybinds. The launcher shows them as buttons above
the settings, beside a Default button of its own (a preset with the id
`default` takes its place); the button whose values the settings have is
lit. Each value must be one its setting takes: in range, one of the choices,
and so on.

```json
"presets": [
  { "id": "easy", "name": "Easy",
    "values": { "damage_taken": 0.5, "enemy_count": 0.75, "mode": "hold", "chaos": false } },
  { "id": "arrows", "name": "Arrow keys",
    "values": { "move_forward": "ArrowUp", "move_back": "ArrowDown" } }
]
```

A preset covers every keybind of the mod and each setting one of its presets
names: the ones of those it does not name go back to their defaults. A
setting no preset names (a Trace switch, a seed) keeps the player's value.

## Reading them

| | |
|---|---|
| Luau | `openrac.setting("mode")`: a boolean, number or string; `nil` for a key the manifest does not declare |
| C++ | `mod.setting<std::string>("mode")`, `setting<bool>`, `setting<int>`, `setting<double>`, ... |
| C | `api->setting_string(mod, "mode")`, `setting_bool`, `setting_int`, `setting_float` |

A keybind reads as a string (`setting_string`, `setting<std::string>`); in C and
C++ `openrac_bind_from_name_n` (`openrac/keys.h`) turns each name into a bind.

A value that is missing, of the wrong type or out of range is the default:
your code always gets a valid value.

Where the values are kept: [where mods live](where-mods-live.md)
(`plugins.json`).

guides.title: Hooks
guides.markdown:
# Hooks

A mod changes what the game does at **hook points**: functions of the game that
OpenRAC lets mods take over. With no mod on a hook point, the game's own code
runs, exactly as on the console.

## Four ways to use a hook point

| | What your function does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **wrap** | does something, calls `original`, maybe does more after | change an argument, then let the game go on |
| **replace** | never calls `original` | write a behaviour anew |
| **before** | runs before the rest; the game's code always runs | count jumps |
| **after** | runs after the rest | read the result, nudge a value |

In Luau, `openrac.hook(id, fn)` wraps or replaces (`fn(original, ...)`), and
`openrac.before` and `openrac.after` take a plain function. In C and C++, a
hook is a wrap or a replace; before and after are a wrap that calls
`original` first or last.

```lua
openrac.hook("rac1.player.set_planar_velocity", function(original, angle)
    original(angle)   -- the game's own, or the mod before yours
    openrac.log(`moving along {angle}`)
end)

openrac.after("rac1.player.advance_animation", function()
    -- runs after the game has moved the animation on
end)
```

## Several mods on one hook point

Mods on the same hook point form a chain, in the order of the Mods tab. The
mod **lower** in the list (loaded later) runs **first**, and its `original`
is the mod above it, down to the game's code. So:

- a mod that calls `original` lets the others run too;
- a mod that does not call `original` stops the chain there; the launcher
  shows when mods share a hook point, so players can order them;
- script and native mods share the same chain.

Take hooks only while your mod loads (in `openrac_mod_load`, in your C++
`load`, or at the top level of a script). Hook points are the same on every
disc a mod supports.

## Stable ids

Every hook point has a permanent **id** of the form
`<game>.<area>.<name>`. Ids never change, even when OpenRAC renames the game
function behind them (the decompilation renames functions as it learns what
they do, and the port's code is moving to C++). Write ids in new mods.

The names hook points had first (`Hero_TurnToHeading`, from the
decompilation) stay as **aliases**: a mod written with one keeps loading.

| Id | Alias | What the game does there |
|---|---|---|
| `rac1.pad.process_report` | `Pad_ProcessReport` | turns one pad report into the pad's state, each poll |
| `rac1.player.update_motion_input` | `Hero_UpdateMotionInput` | reads the stick into the hero, early in his update |
| `rac1.player.turn_to_heading` | `Hero_TurnToHeading` | eases the hero's facing toward where he moves |
| `rac1.player.set_planar_velocity` | `Hero_SetPlanarVelocity` | sets his ground velocity along an angle |
| `rac1.camera.follow.apply_overrides` | `FollowCamera_ApplyOverrides` | the follow camera's per-tick requests from the hero's state |
| `rac1.player.advance_animation` | `Hero_AdvanceAnimation` | moves his animation on, once a tick |

The [reference](reference/hooks-rac1.md) lists every hook point with its
signature and parameters, generated from OpenRAC's table.

## Moby updates (experimental)

The behaviour catalogue lists the game's moby classes (crates, enemies, ...),
their update functions and their per-class variables (pvars). A class's update
is a hook point with the id `rac1.moby.<class>.update` (alias
`Moby_<Class>_Update`), once OpenRAC has made it one. Several classes may share
one update function: check the moby's class in your hook. This part names the
game's internals and is **experimental**: names, fields and signatures may
change as the decompilation goes on.

## What a hook cannot do

- Hook a function OpenRAC has not made a hook point. Ask for one in an
  [issue](https://github.com/OpenRAC/OpenRAC/issues): adding a hook point
  changes nothing for players without mods.
- Take a hook point after load, or let go of one.
- Keep pointers into the game's memory across levels: a level moves its data.

guides.title: Script mods (Luau)
guides.markdown:
# Script mods (Luau)

New in interface 1.1 (SDK 1.1). A script mod is a folder of
[Luau](https://luau.org) files and a manifest. It needs no compiler, runs on
every platform OpenRAC runs on, Android included, and is sandboxed: it sees
only the `openrac` table and the safe parts of Luau's library.

Start from the SDK's `template-script/` ([getting started](getting-started.md)).

## How it runs

At the game's start, each file the manifest's `scripts` lists runs once, in
order. That first run is when the mod takes its hooks and callbacks; after it,
the game calls them.

```lua
--!strict
local swap = openrac.setting("pair") :: string

openrac.on_pad(function(port: number, report: buffer)
    local buttons = buffer.readu16(report, 0)   -- a bit is clear while its button is held
    -- ... change buttons ...
    buffer.writeu16(report, 0, buttons)
end)

openrac.on_frame(function()
    -- after each game tick: 50 a second on PAL, 60 on NTSC-U
end)
```

## The `openrac` table

| | |
|---|---|
| `openrac.game`, `.version`, `.platform`, `.api` | `"rac1"`, `"pal"` or `"ntsc"`, `"macos-arm64"` ..., the game's interface version (`"1.1"`) |
| `openrac.log(...)`, `openrac.warn(...)` | a line in the game's log, after your mod's id (`print` does the same as `log`) |
| `openrac.setting(key)` | one of your [settings](settings.md) |
| `openrac.hook(id, fn)` | wrap or replace a hook point: `fn(original, ...)` gets its arguments; `original(...)` goes on down the chain and returns its result; `original()` with no arguments passes the call's own; return nothing to keep the original's result |
| `openrac.before(id, fn)`, `openrac.after(id, fn)` | `fn(...)` before or after the rest of the chain, which runs whatever `fn` does |
| `openrac.on_frame(fn)` | `fn()` after each game tick |
| `openrac.on_pad(fn)` | `fn(port, report)` for each pad report before the game reads it; `report` is a `buffer` you may change |
| `openrac.fields` | game state by name, read and written as plain values: `openrac.fields.bolts`, `openrac.fields.hero.position.x` (experimental: see the [reference](reference/hooks-rac1.md#fields)) |
| `openrac.read(type, address)`, `openrac.write(type, address, value)` | game memory; `type` is `u8 i8 u16 i16 u32 i32 f32`; addresses in game RAM only (below 32 MB) |
| `openrac.pvars(moby)` | with the behaviour catalogue: the per-class variables of the moby at that address, by name (experimental) |
| `openrac.key(bind)`, `openrac.pressed(bind)` (1.2) | whether a key, mouse button or wheel direction is held, or went down since the last tick, by its name: `openrac.key("KeyW")`, `openrac.pressed("MouseLeft")`, `openrac.pressed("WheelUp")` ([settings](settings.md#key-bindings)) |
| `openrac.mouse()` (1.2) | `dx, dy, wheel_x, wheel_y`: the mouse's motion since the last tick and its wheel in notches |
| `openrac.window()` (1.2) | `focused, captured, overlay`: the window has the keyboard; the cursor is captured; OpenRAC's overlay has the input |
| `openrac.pointer()` (1.3) | `x, y, inside`: the cursor over the game's picture, 0..1 each way (`x * 512`, `y * 416` is the game's 2D pixel), and whether it is over it |
| `openrac.take_input("keyboard")` (1.2) | while your scripts first run: the port's own keyboard table stops pressing pad 0's buttons, so your `on_pad` presses them |
| `openrac.capture_mouse(on)` (1.2) | hide the cursor and keep it in the window (relative motion), or let it go |
| `require(name)` | another `.luau` file of your mod's own folder: `require("util")`, `require("lib/util")` |

Hook points are named by their [ids](hooks.md#stable-ids)
(`"rac1.player.turn_to_heading"`); the older names work too. The full list,
with each one's arguments, is the [reference](reference/luau-api.md).

## The pad report

`on_pad`'s buffer is the controller's report, 18 bytes:

| Bytes | |
|---|---|
| 0-1 | the buttons, a little-endian 16-bit word; a bit is **clear** while its button is held. Bits 0-7: Select, L3, R3, Start, Up, Right, Down, Left; bits 8-15: L2, R2, L1, R1, Triangle, Circle, Cross, Square |
| 2-5 | right stick x, y; left stick x, y (0-255, 128 at rest) |
| 6-17 | pressures (0-255): right, left, up, down, triangle, circle, cross, square, L1, R1, L2, R2 |

## The sandbox

Available: `math`, `string`, `table`, `buffer`, `bit32`, `utf8`, `vector`,
`coroutine`, `os.clock`, `debug.traceback`, `print`. Not available: `io`, the
rest of `os`, `load`, `loadstring`, `dofile`, `getfenv`, `setfenv`, and files
outside your mod's folder. Library tables and `openrac` are read-only, and each
mod has a Luau state of its own, so mods cannot see each other's globals.

## The time budget

Each call into your script (the first run, a hook, a callback) may take at most
2 ms (time spent in the game's own code through `original` does not count).
A script that runs longer, or raises an error, is stopped:

- the error and its traceback go to the game's log, after your mod's id;
- the mod is marked `failed` with the reason in `status.json`, and the
  launcher shows it ([troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md));
- its hooks pass straight to the original from then on, and its callbacks stop.

The game carries on. Keep per-tick work small, and spread long work over
several ticks.

## Autocomplete

The SDK's `types/rac1.d.luau` declares the `openrac` table with every hook
point and field. With [luau-lsp](https://github.com/JohnnyMorganz/luau-lsp),
pass it as a definitions file; the script template's `.vscode/settings.json`
does that for VS Code.

## Packaging

A script mod has nothing to build: its archive is the folder,
`<id>-<version>.zip`, for every platform ([packaging](packaging-and-releases.md)).
From a repository link, the launcher can even install the repository's own
files with no release at all ([install from a link](install-from-link.md)).

guides.title: Native mods in C
guides.markdown:
# Native mods in C

A native mod is a shared library (`.dylib`, `.so`, `.dll`) that the game opens
at start. It talks to the game only through one table of functions, so it is
built against the SDK's headers alone and links against nothing of OpenRAC's.
The C++ layer ([native-cpp.md](native-cpp.md)) is the same thing with less
code; this page is what is underneath.

## The two entry points

```c
#include "openrac/openrac_mod.h"
#include "openrac/games/rac1.h"

OPENRAC_MOD_DEFINE("my-mod", "0.1.0")   /* openrac_mod_query: the interface version, the id */

OPENRAC_MOD_EXPORT int openrac_mod_load(const openrac_api* api, openrac_mod* mod) {
    if (strcmp(api->game, "rac1") != 0) {
        api->fail(mod, "this mod is for Ratchet & Clank");
        return 1;                          /* not loaded; the reason is shown */
    }
    api->log(mod, OPENRAC_LOG_INFO, "hello");
    return 0;                              /* loaded */
}
```

- `openrac_mod_query` tells the game which interface you built for and your
  mod's id and version; they must match the manifest.
- `openrac_mod_load` gets the table (`openrac_api`) and your mod's handle.
  Return 0 to load; anything else refuses, with the reason you gave `fail`.
- `openrac_mod_unload` (optional) runs when the game exits.

Everything happens on the game's thread.

## Hooks

```c
static openrac_rac1_Hero_SetPlanarVelocity s_original;

static void my_velocity(float angle) {
    s_original(angle);   /* the game's own, or the mod before yours */
}

/* in openrac_mod_load: */
if (OPENRAC_RAC1_HOOK(api, mod, Hero_SetPlanarVelocity, my_velocity, &s_original) != OPENRAC_HOOK_OK) {
    api->fail(mod, "no Hero_SetPlanarVelocity in this OpenRAC");
    return 1;
}
```

`api->hook(mod, name, signature, replacement, &original)` takes a hook point
by its id or alias; the signature (`"void(f32)"`) must be the hook point's, or
the call fails. `original` is what your replacement goes on to. See
[hooks](hooks.md) for the chain and the ids, and the
[reference](reference/hooks-rac1.md) for every hook point's signature.

Results: `OPENRAC_HOOK_OK`, `OPENRAC_HOOK_UNKNOWN` (no such hook point here),
`OPENRAC_HOOK_SIGNATURE` (another signature), `OPENRAC_HOOK_TOO_LATE` (outside
load).

## Callbacks

```c
static void tick(void* user) { /* after each game tick */ }
static void pad(void* user, int port, uint8_t* report, int size) { /* change report[] */ }

api->on_frame(mod, tick, NULL);
api->on_pad(mod, pad, NULL);
```

The pad report's layout is in [scripts.md](scripts.md#the-pad-report).

## The keyboard and mouse

Interface 1.2 (`"api": "1.2"`) lets a mod read the keyboard and mouse and
press the pad's buttons from them, for a mod that plays the game with a
keyboard and mouse (rac1-mods' keyboard-mouse):

```c
#include "openrac/keys.h"   /* names for keys, mouse buttons and the wheel */

static int s_jump;          /* a bind: from a keybind setting (settings.md) */

static void pad(void* user, int port, uint8_t* report, int size) {
    const openrac_input* in = s_api->input();      /* this tick's keys and mouse */
    if (port == 0 && openrac_bind_held(in, s_jump)) {
        report[1] &= (uint8_t)~0x40;               /* Cross held (bit 14: a clear bit is held) */
    }
    /* in->mouse_dx, mouse_dy: the motion since the last tick; wheel_x, wheel_y in notches */
}

/* in openrac_mod_load: */
s_jump = openrac_bind_from_name(api->setting_string(mod, "jump"));  /* one bind; split a pair at ',' */
api->take_input(mod, OPENRAC_INPUT_KEYBOARD);  /* the port's own WASD table stops */
api->capture_mouse(mod, 1);                     /* hidden cursor, relative motion */
```

- `input()` is the state for the tick about to run, the same for every call
  in that tick (`in->tick` says which). Each key, `keys[usage]`, has
  `OPENRAC_KEY_HELD` and `OPENRAC_KEY_PRESSED` (it went down since the last
  tick, so a tap shorter than a tick still counts). Nothing is held while the
  window has no focus.
- `take_input` gives the keyboard to your mod: the port's table (WASD, IJKL,
  Space, ...) no longer presses pad 0's buttons. A gamepad still does, so
  merge your buttons into the report rather than overwrite it.
- `capture_mouse` asks; the port lets the cursor go anyway while the window
  has no focus or its overlay (F3) is open (`in->overlay`), and captures it
  again after.
- The game's state (playing, paused, a menu) is the game's own: read it from
  game memory.
- Interface 1.3 adds the cursor over the game's picture: `in->pointer_x`,
  `pointer_y` (0..1 of the 4:3 picture; times 512 and 416, the game's 2D
  pixel) and `pointer_inside`. Check `in->size` covers them first.

## Settings and logging

`api->setting_bool/int/float/string(mod, key)` ([settings](settings.md)), and
`api->log(mod, level, text)` with `OPENRAC_LOG_DEBUG`, `_INFO`, `_WARN`,
`_ERROR`.

## Game memory and functions (experimental)

These name the game's internals: what is where changes with the disc and with
the decompilation's progress.

- `api->memory` is the base of game memory: address `a` is `api->memory + a`
  (`OPENRAC_GREF(api, uint32_t, a)` reads or writes a word).
- `api->relocate_data(a)` and `api->relocate_level_data(level, a)` give a
  global's address in the code loaded now; ask each time, since a level moves
  its globals. `api->loaded_level()` is the level loaded, -1 for none.
- `api->function(name)` and `api->function_at(address)` find a game function to
  call, by its name in this disc's build or by code address.
- `api->stack_push(size, &saved)` / `api->stack_pop(saved)` give room on the
  game's stack for a call that takes the address of a local.

A mod for both discs keeps a table of the addresses and names it uses on each
and picks one by `api->version` (`"pal"`, `"ntsc"`).

## Building

The SDK's CMake package builds the library with only the entry points visible
and no undefined symbols:

```cmake
find_package(OpenRACMod 1.1 REQUIRED)
openrac_add_mod(my_mod MANIFEST openrac-mod.json SOURCES src/mod.c)
```

The full list of the table's members is the [reference](reference/c-api.md).

guides.title: Native mods in C++
guides.markdown:
# Native mods in C++

`openrac/mod.hpp` is a header-only C++17 layer over the C interface
([native-c.md](native-c.md)): hooks as lambdas, typed settings, RAII. It is
compiled into your mod only; the game still sees the C interface, so a C++ mod
works with any OpenRAC of its interface version. The SDK's `template/` is a
C++ mod.

## A whole mod

```cpp
#include "openrac/mod.hpp"
#include "openrac/games/rac1.hpp"

static void load(openrac::Mod& mod) {
    if (mod.game() != "rac1") throw openrac::Error("this mod is for Ratchet & Clank");

    const bool trace = mod.setting<bool>("trace");

    mod.hook<openrac::rac1::Hero_TurnToHeading>(
        [trace, &mod](auto original, int32_t m, float accel, float damping, float limit) {
            if (trace) mod.info("turning");
            original(m, accel, damping, limit);
        });

    mod.on_frame([] { /* after each game tick */ });
}

OPENRAC_MOD_CPP("my-mod", "0.1.0", load)
```

`OPENRAC_MOD_CPP(id, version, load)` writes both entry points. Throwing out of
`load` refuses the mod with the exception's message.

## `openrac::Mod`

| | |
|---|---|
| `game()`, `version()`, `platform()`, `openrac_version()`, `api_major()`, `api_minor()` | about the game running |
| `debug/info/warn/error(text)`, `log(level, text)` | the game's log |
| `fail(reason)` | refuse during load (or throw `openrac::Error`) |
| `setting<T>(key)` | `bool`; an integer type for `int`; `float` or `double`; `std::string` for `choice` and `string` |
| `hook<HookPoint>(callable)` | `callable(original, args...)`; throws `openrac::Error` if the hook point is missing, has another signature, or is taken twice |
| `original<HookPoint>()` | what your hook goes on to, to call it from elsewhere |
| `on_frame(callable)`, `on_pad(callable)` | `callable()`; `callable(port, report, size)` |
| `memory()` | an `openrac::Memory`: `read<T>(address)`, `write<T>(address, value)`, `ref<T>(address)` (experimental) |
| `function<Fn>(name)`, `required_function<Fn>(name)`, `function_at<Fn>(address)` | game functions (experimental) |
| `relocate(address)`, `relocate_level(level, address)`, `loaded_level()` | globals in the code loaded now (experimental) |
| `input()` (1.2) | an `openrac::Input` for the tick about to run: `held(bind)`, `pressed(bind)`, `mouse_dx()`, `mouse_dy()`, `wheel_x()`, `wheel_y()`, `focused()`, `captured()`, `overlay()`, `tick()`; 1.3: `has_pointer()`, `pointer_x()`, `pointer_y()`, `pointer_inside()` ([the keyboard and mouse](native-c.md#the-keyboard-and-mouse)) |
| `take_input(devices)` (1.2) | during load: `OPENRAC_INPUT_KEYBOARD` turns the port's own keyboard table off |
| `capture_mouse(on)` (1.2) | the cursor captured or let go |
| `openrac::bind_from_name(name)`, `openrac::bind_name(bind)` | a key, button or wheel direction by its name (`"KeyW"`, `"MouseLeft"`) |

The hook point types (`openrac::rac1::Hero_TurnToHeading`, ...) are in
`openrac/games/rac1.hpp`, generated from OpenRAC's hook table; see the
[reference](reference/hooks-rac1.md) and [hooks](hooks.md) for ids and chains.

`openrac::StackFrame frame(mod, 16);` gives 16 bytes on the game's stack at
`frame.address()`, given back when `frame` goes out of scope.

## Exceptions never cross into the game

Every hook and callback the layer installs catches whatever your code throws:

- in a hook, the exception is logged with your mod's id and the original runs,
  so the game goes on (if you threw after calling the original, it runs twice:
  do not throw there);
- in a callback, it is logged and the callback returns;
- in `load`, it becomes the refusal.

## Building

```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(my_mod LANGUAGES C CXX)
find_package(OpenRACMod 1.1 REQUIRED)
openrac_add_mod(my_mod MANIFEST openrac-mod.json SOURCES src/mod.cpp)
```

C++17, with each platform's default runtime (libc++ on macOS, libstdc++ on
Linux, the DLL runtime `/MD` with MSVC); only the entry points are exported.
The full API is the [reference](reference/cpp-api.md).

guides.title: Packaging and releases
guides.markdown:
# Packaging and releases

Players install a mod from a `.zip`, or from your repository's address, which
downloads the `.zip` from a release. The SDK makes the archives and the
templates' workflow publishes them, so releasing is pushing a tag.

## The archives

| Archive | What is in it | Made by |
|---|---|---|
| `<id>-<version>-<platform>.zip` | a native mod built for one platform (`windows-x86_64`, `linux-x86_64`, `macos-arm64`, ...) | `package_mod.py build/package/<target>` after a build |
| `<id>-<version>.zip` | a native mod for every platform built, joined; or a script mod (for all platforms) | `package_mod.py --merge ...`; `package_mod.py <folder>` for a script mod |
| `SHA256SUMS` | the SHA-256 of every archive, as `sha256sum` writes it | the workflow |

Inside, the manifest is at the top of the archive (or of its one top folder),
with a native mod's libraries under `lib/<platform>/`, plus `README*` and
`LICENSE*`.

```sh
python3 <SDK>/tools/package_mod.py build/package/my_mod -o dist              # dist/my-mod-0.1.0-macos-arm64.zip
python3 <SDK>/tools/package_mod.py --merge dist/my-mod-0.1.0-*.zip -o dist/my-mod-0.1.0.zip
python3 <SDK>/tools/package_mod.py path/to/script-mod -o dist                # dist/button-swap-1.0.0.zip
python3 <SDK>/tools/package_mod.py --check openrac-mod.json                  # the manifest only
```

`package_mod.py` refuses a manifest the launcher would refuse, so a mod that
packages also installs.

## The workflow

Both templates (`template/` and `template-script/`) carry
`.github/workflows/build.yml`. On every push it:

1. builds and tests native mods (if the repository has a top
   `CMakeLists.txt`) on Windows (MSVC), Linux (x86_64, aarch64) and macOS
   (arm64, x86_64), against the SDK `sdk.lock` pins;
2. packages each platform's build, and every script mod;
3. joins each native mod's platforms, and writes `SHA256SUMS`;
4. keeps them as the run's artifacts.

On a **tag** it also publishes them on that tag's GitHub release.

## Releasing

1. Set `version` in `openrac-mod.json` (and in your `OPENRAC_MOD_CPP` or
   `OPENRAC_MOD_DEFINE` line for a native mod: the game checks they agree).
2. Commit, then tag and push:

   ```sh
   git tag v1.2.0
   git push origin v1.2.0
   ```

   In a repository of several mods released apart, tag `<id>-v<version>`
   (`lock-strafe-v1.2.0`): that release carries only that mod's archives, and a
   `SHA256SUMS` listing them. `v<version>` releases every mod.
3. When the workflow finishes, the release has the archives and `SHA256SUMS`,
   and players' launchers offer the update.

The launcher installs only an archive that `SHA256SUMS` lists with the same
hash, so do not upload archives to a release by hand.

## The SDK your repository builds with

`sdk.lock` names the SDK release (version, address, SHA-256), and
`tools/fetch_sdk.py` downloads it into `.sdk/` and checks it. A new template's
lock has no hash yet: the first fetch takes it from the release and writes it
in; commit `sdk.lock` then. To move to a newer SDK, change its version, address
and hash (each SDK release's notes give the hash).

guides.title: Install from a link
guides.markdown:
# Install from a link

Players add your mod by pasting your repository's address in the launcher's
**Mods** tab (**Add from a link**). This page is what your repository needs for
that, and what the launcher does.

## What players can paste

- `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>` (with or without `.git` or a trailing `/`)
- `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/tree/<branch>`: that branch
- `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/tag/<tag>`: that release

The repository must be **public**: the launcher reads it without an account.

## What your repository needs

- **The manifest**, where the launcher looks for it:
  - one mod: `openrac-mod.json` at the top;
  - several mods: one folder per mod at the top, each with its
    `openrac-mod.json` (as [rac1-mods](https://github.com/OpenRAC/rac1-mods));
  - or a top-level `openrac-mods.json`, `{"format": 1, "mods": ["a", "b"]}`,
    listing the folders to read (then only those).
- **For a native mod, a release** with `<id>-<version>-<platform>.zip` for
  each platform and `SHA256SUMS`: the templates' workflow makes them on a tag
  ([packaging and releases](packaging-and-releases.md)). Players never build
  anything.
- **For a script mod**, a release is optional: without one, the launcher takes
  the mod's folder from the repository itself, at its newest commit.

Both templates are laid out this way already.

## What the launcher does

1. Reads your latest release (or the one linked), the files of the repository
   at its tag, and each manifest.
2. Shows each mod before anything is installed: its name, version and author,
   the repository and its owner, the games and discs it is for, whether this
   OpenRAC can load it (and why not), and what it runs: **Runs scripts
   (sandboxed)** for a script mod, a warning that it runs code on this computer
   for a native mod.
3. On **Install**:
   - a native mod: downloads the archive for the player's platform, checks it
     against `SHA256SUMS`, and checks that the manifest inside is the one
     shown;
   - a script mod: the release's `<id>-<version>.zip` if there is one
     (checked the same way), else the repository's own files;
   - then installs it as an archive added by hand would be, switched on.
4. Remembers where it came from, for updates.

It refuses, with the reason: a mod with no archive for this platform, no
`SHA256SUMS` or a hash that differs, a manifest inside that is not the one
shown, a mod for another game.

## Updates and pinning

**Check for updates** (and once a day by itself) looks for a newer release
with an archive for the player's platform, or, for a script mod with no
releases, a newer commit. The mod's row then offers **Update**; an update keeps
its place in the list, its switch and its settings. A player can choose **Keep
this version** to never be offered one.

## Other git hosts

From other hosts the launcher installs mods without a build (script mods, data
packs) through `git`, when the player has it installed. Native mods need
releases, which it reads from GitHub today.

guides.title: Where mods live
guides.markdown:
# Where mods live

Everything is in the player's own folders, never in the launcher's (which is
read-only when installed: an AppImage, the macOS app, the Windows installer's
folder). The launcher keeps its games in an **install folder**, shown in its
Settings; by default:

| System | Install folder | A game's mods |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | `~/OpenRAC` | `~/OpenRAC/active/rac1/data/plugins/` |
| macOS | `~/OpenRAC` | `~/OpenRAC/active/rac1/data/plugins/` |
| Windows | `%USERPROFILE%\OpenRAC` | `%USERPROFILE%\OpenRAC\active\rac1\data\plugins\` |

(If that folder cannot be made, the launcher's own data folder:
`~/.local/share/dev.openrac.launcher`, `~/Library/Application
Support/dev.openrac.launcher`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\dev.openrac.launcher`.)

## Inside `plugins/`

```
plugins/
├── plugins.json     the mods' order, which are on, their settings (the launcher writes it)
├── status.json      what the game did with each mod at its last start (the game writes it)
├── sources.json     where mods installed from a link came from, for updates
└── <id>/            one mod, as installed: openrac-mod.json, scripts or lib/<platform>/...
```

`plugins.json`:

```json
{
  "format": 1,
  "mods": [
    { "id": "lock-strafe", "enabled": true, "settings": { "mode": "lock" } },
    { "id": "button-swap", "enabled": false, "settings": {} }
  ]
}
```

The order of `mods` is the load order ([hooks](hooks.md)). A folder that is not
listed shows in the launcher, off.

## How the game finds them

The launcher starts the game with `--data <the game's data folder>` and
`--plugins <data>/plugins/plugins.json`, or `--no-mods` in purist mode. Neither
side guesses a path. Run by hand without `--plugins`, the game reads
`<data>/plugins/plugins.json`.

## Without the launcher

Copy your mod's folder to `plugins/<id>/` and add it to `plugins.json`. This is
also the quickest way to try a change: edit the files in place and restart the
game.

## Android

The game runs inside the app there, and Android does not let an app load code it
wrote itself, so native mods are not loaded on Android. Script mods are.

guides.title: Troubleshooting
guides.markdown:
# Troubleshooting

## The mod is on but does nothing

1. **Look at its row in the Mods tab.** A mod that cannot load says why there,
   before Play (another disc, an interface this OpenRAC lacks, no library for
   this computer, a missing or conflicting mod) and after it (what happened at
   the last start).
2. **Read `status.json`** in the game's `plugins/` folder
   ([where mods live](where-mods-live.md)). For each mod that is on:

   | `state` | Meaning |
   |---|---|
   | `loaded` | running; `hooks` lists what it took |
   | `refused` | a check failed before it was opened; `reason` says which |
   | `failed` | its library could not be opened, its load refused (with your `fail` reason), it asked for a hook point this OpenRAC does not have or with another signature, or (a script) it raised an error or ran over its time budget: `reason` has the message |

   `hook_points` lists every hook point this OpenRAC has.
3. **Read the game's log** (**Logs** on the game's page): its header has a
   `mods` line naming the mods loaded, and your mod's lines start with its id.
   A script's errors are there with their traceback.

## Common reasons

| Reason | What to do |
|---|---|
| needs interface 1.1; this OpenRAC has 1.0 | the player needs a newer OpenRAC, or set `api` to what you really use |
| not for this disc | add the disc to `games` if the mod works there |
| no library for this platform | build for it (the template's workflow builds all desktop ones), or it is Android, which loads only script mods |
| no hook point X | check its [id](hooks.md#stable-ids), or ask for the hook point |
| signature differs | the hook point's signature is in the [reference](reference/hooks-rac1.md) |
| stopped while the game ran: hook X: ... | your script's error, or it ran over its 2 ms budget |

## Purist mode

The launcher's **Purist mode** (in Settings and on the Mods tab) starts the game
with no mods at all (`--no-mods`): the game as on the console, with only
OpenRAC's own fixes. Ask players to try it first when they report a problem.

## When the game crashes

The crash report (the game page's **Logs and crash reports**) lists every mod
that was loaded, and names the one whose code was running when it can tell: a
native mod's library, or the script mod being called. The launcher's crash
notice suggests trying again in purist mode when mods were on.

## Asking for help

Open an issue at [OpenRAC](https://github.com/OpenRAC/OpenRAC/issues) with the
mod's `status.json`, the log, and the crash report if there is one; the reports
leave out the player's home folder.

guides.title: Views of the game (VR and other displays)
guides.markdown:
# Views of the game (VR and other displays)

Interface 1.4 lets a native mod draw the game a second way besides the
window: the two eyes of a VR headset, a panel with the HUD, a second screen.
The port draws each view from the same scene as the window's picture and
copies it where the mod says. The mod owns everything else: the headset, its
runtime (OpenXR), its controllers. OpenRAC links no VR library.

Nothing here runs unless a mod asks for it. A game with no such mod draws as
before.

## What the port offers

| Call | When | What |
|---|---|---|
| `graphics()` | any time | What the port draws with (`openrac_graphics`): OpenGL, OpenGL ES or Vulkan. OpenGL gives `gl_proc`. Vulkan gives the instance, physical device, device and queue, with the queue's family and index |
| `on_views(mod, &source)` | during load | Draw views each frame through `source` (`openrac_view_source`): `begin`, `end`, optional `closing`. One mod at a time |
| `setup_vulkan(mod, &setup)` | during load | Make the Vulkan device through `setup` (`openrac_vulkan_setup`), so the mod can share it. One mod at a time |

In C++: `mod.has_views()`, `mod.graphics()`, `mod.on_views(source)` and
`mod.setup_vulkan(setup)`, which throw `openrac::Error` when refused.

## A frame

Each frame the port draws the scene (each refresh, between ticks too) goes
like this:

1. The port records the window's picture.
2. It calls `begin(user, views, max)`. The mod fills up to `max` views
   (`OPENRAC_VIEW_MAX`, 4) and returns how many it filled. With OpenXR this
   is where `xrWaitFrame`, `xrBeginFrame`, `xrLocateViews` and
   `xrAcquireSwapchainImage` go.
3. The port draws each view and copies it into the view's `texture` (OpenGL)
   or `image` (Vulkan).
4. The port shows the window's picture and submits the frame to the GPU.
5. It calls `end(user, views, count)` with the same views. `drawn` is 1 when
   the view was drawn anew. With OpenXR this is where
   `xrReleaseSwapchainImage` and `xrEndFrame` go.

`end` follows every `begin`, even one that returned 0. Frames that show a
movie or a still picture instead of the scene call neither.

## A view

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `kind` | `OPENRAC_VIEW_FULL` (world and 2D), `OPENRAC_VIEW_WORLD` (world only) or `OPENRAC_VIEW_2D` (the 2D alone over transparent black, for a panel; give it a 4:3 shape) |
| `width`, `height` | 1 to 8192 pixels |
| `position`, `orientation` | The eye relative to the game's camera, in its view space (X right, Y up, looking down -Z, as OpenXR's), in game units. Orientation is a quaternion x, y, z, w; all zero is the identity |
| `angle_left`, `angle_right`, `angle_up`, `angle_down` | The field of view as OpenXR's `XrFovf` gives it, in radians. All zero: the game's own vertical one |
| `texture` | OpenGL: a `GL_TEXTURE_2D` of the port's context, RGBA8 or SRGB8_ALPHA8, at least the view's size |
| `image`, `image_layout` | Vulkan: a `VkImage` of the port's device, `R8G8B8A8_UNORM` or `_SRGB`, exactly the view's size, usable as a transfer destination; the layout it is in, which it is left in |
| `drawn`, `picture` | Set by the port: drawn anew this frame; the port's own GL texture of the view |

The picture is copied byte for byte. An sRGB image gets the game's picture as
the window shows it.

The game decides what it draws (mobys out of its view are not drawn), so a
mod turning the view far from the game's camera should also move the game's
camera through its hooks. The eye's pose is for the small offsets: the eyes'
distance, the head's last movement.

## Vulkan

OpenXR needs the Vulkan device made with it
(`xrCreateVulkanInstanceKHR`, `xrGetVulkanGraphicsDevice2KHR`,
`xrCreateVulkanDeviceKHR`). The window makes the device, so a mod that does
this:

- says `"vulkan_device": true` in its manifest, so that the mods load before
  the window opens (without it they load after, as before);
- calls `setup_vulkan` in its load with the functions that stand in for
  `vkCreateInstance`, the choice of the physical device and `vkCreateDevice`;
  each is optional;
- gets the device back from `graphics()` once the window is open, for
  `XrGraphicsBindingVulkanKHR`.

When `create_instance` or `create_device` fails, or the chosen device cannot
draw the game, the game draws with OpenGL instead. Check `graphics()`.

While a mod has views, the Vulkan renderer draws on the game's thread: the
port then submits to the queue only from there, where the mod's callbacks
run, so OpenXR calls that use the queue need no lock.

The player picks Vulkan with `OPENRAC_GL_API=vulkan`; OpenGL is the default on
desktops.

## Closing

`closing` is called once, before the graphics context goes: destroy the
OpenXR session and swapchains there. The views end with it.

## Limits

- A view skips the window's ambient occlusion and temporal upscaling. With
  enhanced rendering on, a view of another size than the window remakes the
  enhanced lighting's targets each frame, which costs time.
- The views' textures are found by their GL name: keep a texture alive while
  it is used (an OpenXR swapchain's images are, for the session).
- Script mods have no views.

c.intro:
The interface between OpenRAC's native port and a native mod (docs/port/MODS.md).

A mod is a shared library (.dylib, .so, .dll) that exports openrac_mod_query and openrac_mod_load,
and optionally openrac_mod_unload. The port opens it at start, before the game runs, asks
openrac_mod_query which interface it was built for, and calls openrac_mod_load with the table of
what the port offers (openrac_api). The mod uses nothing of the port but that table: it is built
against this header alone, and links against nothing of OpenRAC's.

Versions. OPENRAC_MOD_API_MAJOR changes when anything in the table changes or goes: a mod built
for another major is refused. OPENRAC_MOD_API_MINOR grows when something is added at the end of
the table: a mod built for a minor above the port's is refused, one built for a lower minor loads
(and checks api->api_minor before it uses anything newer than what it was built for).

Everything runs on the game's thread: load, the hooks, the callbacks, unload.

This header is plain C (C99, and C++ through its extern "C" block): it is the ABI, and the C++
layer (openrac/mod.hpp) is built on it. It is laid out as: versions, helper macros, types,
the input state, the table (openrac_api), the entry points, then the helpers a mod uses.
Each item says which interface version added it ("Since 1.0" is the original table); a mod
checks api->api_minor before it uses anything newer than the minor it was built for.

sections.title: The world: the level's mobys
sections.about: For a mod that shares the world between games: one game runs it (its enemies, crates, doors, platforms), the others drive their copies from it. A moby is named by its slot (its index in the level's moby array, this game's own) and, when the level placed it, by its key (its record in the level's file: the same moby has the same key in every game that loads the level, whatever was killed before). A driven moby's own update no longer runs (its animation still plays and its collision follows it): the mod poses it. The gate (on_moby_update) is asked around each update the game runs; before one, the mod may have the hero stand in elsewhere for it (another player: the enemy then sees, chases and hits that player's figure). Hits the game posts are told to a mod (on_moby_hit), which may take them back, and a mod posts its own (moby_hit).

examples.code:
*
 * An example mod that uses each part of the interface (sdk/README.md): it refuses a game it is not
 * for, reads a bool and an int setting, counts the game's ticks with on_frame, and takes a hook
 * point, counting the calls and going on to what it replaced. Every `every` ticks it logs both
 * counts. It changes nothing in the game.
 *
 * How it works: OPENRAC_MOD_DEFINE writes openrac_mod_query; openrac_mod_load keeps the table and
 * the handle in file-level variables (the port calls the mod's functions on the game's thread, one
 * at a time, so no lock is needed), takes the hook point and the callback, and logs a line;
 * openrac_mod_unload logs the totals at exit. Written in C, so the whole mod is plain C99 against
 * openrac_mod.h and games/rac1.h.
 */

members.name: log
members.about: a line in the game's log, after your mod's id (`print` does the same as `log`)

examples.code:
openrac.hook("rac1.player.set_planar_velocity", function(original, angle)
    original(angle)   -- the game's own, or the mod before yours
    openrac.log(`moving along {angle}`)
end)

openrac.after("rac1.player.advance_animation", function()
    -- runs after the game has moved the animation on
end)

-- After each game tick (50 a second on PAL, 60 on NTSC-U).
openrac.on_frame(function()
	ticks += 1
	if ticks % (every * 50) == 0 then
		openrac.log(`still here after {ticks} ticks`)
	end
end)

members.name: warn

local swap = openrac.setting("pair") :: string

    local buttons = buffer.readu16(report, 0)   -- a bit is clear while its button is held
    -- ... change buttons ...
    buffer.writeu16(report, 0, buttons)
end)

openrac.on_frame(function()
    -- after each game tick: 50 a second on PAL, 60 on NTSC-U
end)

local every = openrac.setting("every") :: number -- the manifest's setting, as the launcher set it
local ticks = 0

members.name: hook
members.about: wrap or replace a hook point: `fn(original, ...)` gets its arguments; `original(...)` goes on down the chain and returns its result; `original()` with no arguments passes the call's own; return nothing to keep the original's result

examples.code:

    original(angle)   -- the game's own, or the mod before yours
    openrac.log(`moving along {angle}`)
end)

openrac.after("rac1.player.advance_animation", function()
    -- runs after the game has moved the animation on
end)

    local buttons = buffer.readu16(report, 0)   -- a bit is clear while its button is held
    -- ... change buttons ...
    buffer.writeu16(report, 0, buttons)

    -- after each game tick: 50 a second on PAL, 60 on NTSC-U

members.name: read
members.about: game memory; `type` is `u8 i8 u16 i16 u32 i32 f32`; addresses in game RAM only (below 32 MB)

members.name: write
members.about: game memory; `type` is `u8 i8 u16 i16 u32 i32 f32`; addresses in game RAM only (below 32 MB)

members.name: fields
members.about: game state by name, read and written as plain values: `openrac.fields.bolts`, `openrac.fields.hero.position.x` (experimental: see the [reference](reference/hooks-rac1.md#fields))

members.name: key
members.about: whether a key, mouse button or wheel direction is held, or went down since the last tick, by its name: `openrac.key("KeyW")`, `openrac.pressed("MouseLeft")`, `openrac.pressed("WheelUp")` ([settings](settings.md#key-bindings))

members.name: pressed
members.about: whether a key, mouse button or wheel direction is held, or went down since the last tick, by its name: `openrac.key("KeyW")`, `openrac.pressed("MouseLeft")`, `openrac.pressed("WheelUp")` ([settings](settings.md#key-bindings))

members.name: mouse
members.about: `dx, dy, wheel_x, wheel_y`: the mouse's motion since the last tick and its wheel in notches

members.name: window
members.about: `focused, captured, overlay`: the window has the keyboard; the cursor is captured; OpenRAC's overlay has the input

members.name: pointer
members.about: `x, y, inside`: the cursor over the game's picture, 0..1 each way (`x * 512`, `y * 416` is the game's 2D pixel), and whether it is over it

members.name: take_input
members.about: while your scripts first run: the port's own keyboard table stops pressing pad 0's buttons, so your `on_pad` presses them

members.name: capture_mouse
members.about: hide the cursor and keep it in the window (relative motion), or let it go

members.name: pvars
members.about: with the behaviour catalogue: the per-class variables of the moby at that address, by name (experimental)

members.name: require
members.about: another `.luau` file of your mod's own folder: `require("util")`, `require("lib/util")`

hooks.name: Pad_ProcessReport
hooks.about: One pad report into the pad's state (PadState, at pad), each poll, before the tick reads it.

hooks.name: Hero_UpdateMotionInput
hooks.about: The stick read into the hero, early in his update each tick.

hooks.name: Hero_TurnToHeading
hooks.about: Eases the hero's facing toward his move yaw.

hooks.name: Hero_SetPlanarVelocity
hooks.about: The hero's velocity at his ground speed along an angle; an angle above pi means his facing.

hooks.name: FollowCamera_ApplyOverrides
hooks.about: The follow camera's per-tick requests from the hero's state; the camera moby's update calls it before it places the eye.

hooks.name: Hero_AdvanceAnimation
hooks.about: Ratchet's animation moved on by his animation speed, once a tick after his state's update.

hooks.name: Item_Give
hooks.about: Gives the player item id (GiveItem): sets its owned and obtained bytes, shows its banner, gives its starting ammo, marks it bought in the vendor's stock and adds it to the quick select; equip non-zero also puts it in hand. Every item the game gives goes through it but the Persuader's.

hooks.name: Planet_Unlock
hooks.about: Unlocks a planet's coordinates (UnlockPlanet): its flag (one byte per level), the galaxy list, and its banner unless it is the planet the player is on.

hooks.name: Vendor_InitLevelStock
hooks.about: The vendor's stock at each level start (VendorStockLevelInit): gives the Bomb Glove while the player has none, keeps the stock's known items and adds the level's new weapon.

hooks.name: Vendor_BuildItemList
hooks.about: The vendor menu's list (VendorBuildItemList), from the stock and the items owned: each time the menu opens and after each purchase. skip_unflagged leaves out what is for sale (the menu opened from the pause screen).

hooks.name: GoldBolts_CountCollected
hooks.about: The gold bolts collected, at most 40 (count_nonzero_entries_up_to_40): what the pause screen shows; the unspent ones are this less 4 per gold weapon.

hooks.name: Hero_TakeDamage
hooks.about: Takes hit points off the hero's health (Hero_TakeDamage): at most one a call, none for 0, then the HUD's health bank. Every hit the hero takes goes through it but the instant kills (falls, crushers), which set his health to 0.

hooks.name: Moby_GetHitMessage
hooks.about: The hit pending on moby (MobyGetHitMessage): the record of the last hit posted to it (+0x20 the attacker, +0x24 the flags, +0x2C the damage, an f32) when its flags match mask, else 0, dropping the hit unless keep. How the hero and every enemy read the hits they take, each tick, so a hit may be read more than once.

hooks.name: Weapon_TakeAmmo
hooks.about: Takes amount of ammo from item for a shot (TakeAmmo; -1 is the item in hand): 1 when taken, 0 when there is too little. An item with no ammo limit takes none and gives 1.

hooks.name: Moby_RecordDeath
hooks.about: Records a placed moby's death or a crate's break (SetDeathBits): its save id's killed bits (none for a save id below 0), its mission, then drops its bolts: about the s16 at +0xB4 (or what a tallied source has left of +0xB6), which it then clears.

hooks.name: Level_LoadGameplay
hooks.about: Loads a level's gameplay file into the level heap (LoadLevelGameplay), once per level start: the settings, the placed mobys and their pvars, the spare moby pool, the paths and the rest; returns the heap cursor. After it, every placed moby exists and none has run.

hooks.name: Hero_ApproachSpeed
hooks.about: Eases the hero's ground speed (+0x194, the speed Hero_SetPlanarVelocity moves him at) toward his target speed (+0x190) by up when below it and by down when above, each tick he moves on foot, in every level.

hooks.name: Ship_TravelTo
hooks.about: The ship's travel from the planet select (ShipTravelTo), once its menu closes: to the planet it is on (dest the level now), the landing again, as backing out of the select does; to another, the game saved to the card and the ship's flight out of the level, whose loop then ends and flies to dest. After the take-off; a level's only way to another planet by ship.

hooks.name: Moby_CollectBolt
hooks.about: Collects a bolt (collect_bolt), called by the bolt update (classes 13 to 16) once the bolt reaches the hero: adds its value (1, or 5 / 20 / 50 for classes 14 / 15 / 16) to the bolt count, the level's total and its source's stats, shows the bolt counter and makes two sparkles at it. The bolt update then deletes the bolt (a placed one marked taken) whether or not this ran.
